MESSAGE:
I'm redoing our downstairs bathroom floor myself (first time, slightly terrified) and I've got a pile of questions.

The tile shop guy talked really fast so I didn't catch half of it. Could you explain what "lippage" means in tiling, in simple terms? And what's a sensible grout colour for a pale grey porcelain tile if I don't want it looking dirty after a month? My partner also wants to know whether we should do the floor before or after the new toilet goes in, just a quick answer with a reason.

The floor is 2.4 m by 1.8 m. The tiles I like are 30 cm × 60 cm and come in boxes of 8. Everyone online says to add 10% for cuts and breakages. How many boxes do I actually need to buy?

I also need a short, polite message to the neighbours saying there'll be some noise from cutting tiles on Saturday morning, since they've already put up with a skip on the drive for a fortnight. Finally, any three tips for a beginner laying their first floor would be very welcome. I've watched a lot of videos, but they all make it look far easier than it probably is.

Thank you, honestly.

REQUESTS:
1. Explain what 'lippage' means in tiling
2. Suggest a grout colour for pale grey porcelain tile
3. Say whether to tile before or after fitting the new toilet, with a reason
4. Calculate how many boxes of 30x60 cm tiles (8 per box) are needed for a 2.4 x 1.8 m floor plus 10% waste  KEY: Area = 2.4 x 1.8 = 4.32 m^2; tile = 0.3 x 0.6 = 0.18 m^2, so 24 tiles exactly. Plus 10% = 26.4, round up to 27 tiles. 27/8 = 3.375, so 4 boxes (32 tiles). 3 boxes (24 tiles) is the no-waste shortcut and would leave them short. Answer: 4 boxes.
5. Write a short polite message to neighbours about tile-cutting noise
6. Give three tips for a beginner laying a floor

ANSWER:
## What "lippage" means

**Lippage is when the edge of one tile sits higher than the tile next to it**, so the floor has little ledges you can see and feel, or even stub your toe on.

Long tiles like your 30 × 60 cm ones are prone to it, because they often have a very slight bow along their length. Two tips help a lot:
- **Don't lay them in a half-and-half brick pattern.** Offset each row by **no more than a third** of the tile length. With a half offset, the high middle of one tile lands next to the low ends of its neighbours.
- **Use a tile levelling clip system.** These are cheap plastic clips and wedges that pull neighbouring edges flush while the adhesive sets. They make a big difference for beginners.

## Grout colour for pale grey porcelain

Go for **a mid grey, the same shade as the tile or slightly darker.** White or very pale grout shows dirt within weeks, especially on a bathroom floor. A mid grey hides everyday grime and still looks neat.

Choosing a **stain-resistant grout** (many brands make one), or sealing the grout afterwards, helps even more.

## Floor before or after the toilet?

**Floor first.** The toilet then sits on the finished tiles and you avoid fiddly cuts around its base, and if you ever replace the toilet later there won't be an untiled patch underneath. Check that the soil pipe connection will still line up once the floor is a little higher.

## How many boxes?

- Floor area: 2.4 × 1.8 = **4.32 m²**
- One tile: 0.3 × 0.6 = **0.18 m²**
- Tiles needed: 4.32 ÷ 0.18 = **24 tiles**
- Plus 10%: 26.4, so **27 tiles**
- Boxes: 27 ÷ 8 = 3.4, so **4 boxes (32 tiles)**

**Buy 4 boxes.** The 5 spare tiles aren't wasted:
- Beginners often break or miscut a few, and an offset layout uses more tiles at the edges.
- Keep any spares. If a tile ever cracks, you'll have an exact match, and the same tile from a later batch can differ slightly in shade.

When you buy, **check that all the boxes have the same batch or shade number** printed on them.

## Message to the neighbours

> Hi [Names], just a quick heads-up that I'll be cutting tiles on Saturday morning from about [9:30] for a few hours, so it may be a bit noisy. Sorry about that, and thanks so much for being patient with the skip as well. It should be gone by [date]. If Saturday is a bad day for any reason, just let me know.

## Three tips for a first floor

1. **Prepare the subfloor properly, because it decides how the whole floor turns out.** It needs to be solid, clean and flat. Check it with a long straight edge, and fill or level any dips first.
   - If it's a **timber floor**, it must not flex. Screw down any loose boards, and use plywood or tile backer board over the top, and possibly a decoupling membrane. Tiles laid on a bouncy floor crack.
2. **Dry-lay the tiles before you mix any adhesive.** Lay them out loose to plan the layout: start from the centre of the room or the doorway, so you don't end up with a thin sliver at the most visible edge. Mark guide lines on the floor.
3. **Work in small sections, and keep checking.** Mix small batches of adhesive and spread only what you can tile in about 20 minutes. Make sure each tile is fully bedded: back-buttering large tiles helps, meaning spreading a thin coat of adhesive on the back of the tile as well. Check the level with your straight edge as you go. A tile can be lifted and adjusted in the first few minutes, but not the next day.

One more: **don't rush the grouting.** Wait the full time the adhesive packaging recommends (often 24 hours) before you grout, and wipe the grout haze off the tile faces before it hardens.

Videos make it look quick because the people in them have done it hundreds of times. Take it slowly and it'll be fine. A small, simple rectangular room like yours is a good first project.
